title: Ionospheric layers, scatter and NVIS
blurb: Explain which layer does what, why the D region blocks low bands by day, and how scatter and NVIS fill the skip zone.

G3C01.why: The layers stack D, E, F1, F2 going up. **D is the lowest**, closest to the surface.

G3C02.why: The critical frequency at a given angle is the **highest frequency still refracted back** to Earth. Higher goes through.
G3C02.trap: That is not a signal-to-noise figure, and it is not the lowest frequency.

G3C03.why: F2 is the **highest** layer, so a hop from it covers the most ground.
G3C03.trap: Height sets the hop length, not density.

G3C04.why: The critical angle is the **highest takeoff angle** that still returns the wave. Steeper than that and the wave escapes.
G3C04.trap: It is not a bearing or azimuth.

G3C05.why: By day the **D region absorbs** signals on 160, 80, 60 and 40 m, so distant contacts are harder.
G3C05.trap: The F region returns these bands. It is not what blocks them.

G3C06.why: Scatter signals arrive weak and mixed, with a **fluttering sound**.
G3C06.trap: Scatter doesn't give clear, high-intelligibility audio and isn't only a night effect.

G3C07.why: Energy reaches the skip zone **through several different paths**, so the audio sounds distorted.

G3C08.why: Only a **small part of the signal energy** is scattered into the skip zone, so it is weak.

G3C09.why: **Scatter** puts weak signals into the transmitter's skip zone, where normal skywave never lands.

G3C10.why: NVIS is **short-distance MF or HF propagation at high elevation angles**: up steeply, back close by.

G3C11.why: In daylight the **D region** absorbs signals below 10 MHz the most.
